sourceUrl: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2602.09345 (v3, cs.OS, 22 Jul 2026; abstract page https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.09345). Full text extracted locally via pdftotext.
statedGuarantee: AgentCgroup bounds CPU and memory consumption of sandboxed AI coding agents at tool-call granularity. Each agent workload maps to a cgroup v2 node with per-tool-call ephemeral child cgroups; enforcement runs in-kernel via sched_ext (CPU) and memcg_bpf_ops (memory throttle delays), applying graduated degradation - throttle via memory.high delay, then freeze via cgroup.freeze - instead of termination, so a high-priority agent session survives memory contention from co-tenant sessions without an OOM kill that would destroy accumulated LLM context. This is a resource/QoS guarantee about how MUCH an agent consumes, NOT an action-authorization guarantee about WHAT an agent may do. The paper states no threat model, names no adversary, and makes no security claim; the word 'isolation' is used throughout in the performance sense (multi-tenant resource isolation), never in the confinement sense.
advertisedRhetoric: "in-kernel enforcement via sched_ext and memcg_bpf_ops"; "AgentCgroup executes control logic directly at kernel cgroup enforcement points via eBPF, enabling microsecond-level reaction without user-kernel round trips"; "No application code is modified; isolation is achieved entirely through container cgroup boundaries and eBPF hooks"; "These primitives enable in-kernel enforcement with microsecond-level reaction times."
tierSpan: Concretely, a transparent bash wrapper intercepts each bash -c invocation, a common tool-call execution interface in agent frameworks, and creates an ephemeral child cgroup (tool_<pid>_<ts>/) for the duration of the command. The wrapper moves the tool process into this child cgroup, collects per-tool-call resource metrics (memory.peak, duration), and removes the cgroup upon exit.
cheapestDefeat: TIER WORKED EXPLICITLY. (1) The guarantee: every tool call executes inside its own resource-bounded cgroup domain whose limits are enforced in kernel. (2) The mechanism that must fail for it not to hold: the transparent userspace bash wrapper that intercepts `bash -c` and MOVES the tool process into the ephemeral child cgroup. The kernel enforces limits only on whatever cgroup a process is actually in; if the wrapper never runs, no per-tool-call cgroup is ever created and no per-tool-call bound exists. (3) Cheapest adversary action: execute the tool by any path that is not a wrapped `bash -c` invocation - a sub-agent tool call (the paper's own second-largest tool type at 17.3% of Haiku tool execution time, and explicitly 'a new agent instance', not a `bash -c`), a direct execve issued by the framework, a Read/Edit tool, or invoking the shell binary by absolute path. This needs no privilege, no kernel exploit, no BPF knowledge, and no framework modification. (4) The mechanism that action defeats is an application-layer chokepoint on the tool-call path -> T3. NOTE the honest residual: processes that evade the wrapper still land in the coarse workload/container cgroup, and THAT bound is genuinely T2. But the container-level bound is exactly the pre-existing baseline the paper's own 'granularity mismatch' (section 4.1) argues is inadequate - so the T2 residual is not the paper's contribution, it is the thing the contribution exists to replace. Scoring the contribution at its weakest link gives T3. Two further ambiguities resolved downward per the conservative stance: the paper never states whether the container's cgroup filesystem is delegated writable to the agent (a writable cgroup.procs would let a process migrate itself out of its domain), and the memcg_bpf_ops hooks it depends on are an unmerged RFC ('currently under upstream review'), so the kernel-side interposition point is not yet a stable kernel guarantee.
placementSpan: We use three agent traces run concurrently in separate cgroups: dask/dask#11628 as the HIGH-priority session (peak 421 MB, memory.high = max) and two instances of sigmavirus24/github3.py#673 as LOW-priority sessions (peak 406 MB each, memory.high = 400 MB). Under BPF, LOW cgroups are throttled when the HIGH cgroup experiences memory pressure; the HIGH cgroup is protected via below_low.

coverageSpans.E7: In Haiku, Bash and the sub-agent tool (which delegates to a new agent instance) together account for over 90% of total tool execution time (80.6% and 17.3% respectively); GLM relies almost entirely on Bash (98.8% of tool time, Fig. 2(a)).

schneider.surrogate: Per-cgroup CPU and memory limits enforced at kernel allocation and scheduling points - a memory.high throttle delay computed by a memcg_bpf_ops hook, cgroup.freeze on a subtree, and sched_ext dispatch prioritization. This is a classic safety property: an execution monitor sits at the allocation/dispatch point and delays or halts the step. Measured behaviorally (100% vs 66% OOM survival; throttle precision within 2.3% relative error against a 2000 ms configured delay).
schneider.objective: Multi-tenant isolation in which all concurrent sessions COMPLETE with accumulated LLM context preserved, achieved by the agent voluntarily reconstructing a less resource-intensive execution strategy after natural-language stderr feedback ('exploits agents' ability to declare resource needs and reconstruct execution strategies'). This is a liveness/behavioral objective over a non-deterministic LLM - a monitor can stop a bad step but cannot compel a good one - and the paper concedes the upward half of the protocol is unenforceable: 'Declarations are advisory; the feedback loop corrects underestimates.' A mis-declaring or non-cooperating agent is corrected only after the fact, if at all.

notes:
ADJUDICATOR-CRITICAL FRAMING. This is a resource-management / QoS paper, not a security paper. It contains no threat model, no adversary, no attacker capability, and no security claim; a grep of the full text returns no occurrence of 'threat', 'adversary', 'malicious', 'attack', 'untrusted', or 'escape'. Every use of 'isolation' is performance isolation between co-tenant workloads. Coding it on the ACTION-SURFACE-v1.1 grid therefore measures something the authors never claimed, and the near-uniform not-covered row is a category fact about the paper's scope, not a criticism of its execution. It should be carried in the corpus as a NEGATIVE/CONTRAST case: the strongest available demonstration that kernel-level hierarchical enforcement is real and reachable, sitting alongside the demonstration that resource-bounding an effector is not the same as mediating it.

WHY E2 IS PARTIAL, NOT COVERED (the cell the corpus asked this paper to test). Two things must both hold for E2 'covered', and only one does. (a) DESCENDANT REACH - genuinely strong, and the useful positive finding. cgroup v2 membership is inherited across fork/clone by the kernel, and the paper confirms the policy attachment inherits too: 'memcg_bpf_ops attached to the parent cgroup automatically applies to all child cgroups via cgroup v2 hierarchy inheritance.' A grandchild process of a tool call cannot shed the resource bound by forking, cannot opt out, and can be stopped wholesale via cgroup.freeze / cgroup.kill / memory.oom.group (the paper notes cgroup.kill 'terminates all processes while handling concurrent forks'). This is exactly the descendant survival that in-process hooks and MCP-layer interposition never achieve - on the resource dimension it IS a T2 property. (b) EFFECTOR REACH - fails twice over. First, AgentCgroup never authorizes or denies a spawn: no subprocess is ever prevented, no spawn is classified allowed/disallowed, and an agent that spawns a subprocess to do something forbidden is entirely unimpeded so long as it stays under its memory ceiling. Second, the ASSIGNMENT of a spawn into its fine-grained domain runs through a bypassable userspace wrapper on one tool-call interface (`bash -c`), so the fine-grained half provably does not reach spawns arriving by other paths. Hierarchical inheritance is only as good as the cgroup you were put in. Partial is the correct and generous reading; a stricter coder could argue not-covered on the grounds that a resource ceiling is not mediation of the spawn effector at all.

WHY E7 IS NOT-COVERED WHILE E2 IS PARTIAL (consistency note). The distinction is whether the paper's own mechanism targets the effector. The bash wrapper by construction wraps a subprocess spawn, so E2 gets partial credit. It explicitly does NOT wrap sub-agent invocation - the paper's own tool taxonomy lists the sub-agent tool as a separate type from Bash, says it 'delegates to a new agent instance', and reports it as the second-largest consumer of Haiku tool time at 17.3%. Sub-agents therefore receive no per-call domain at all; they inherit only the coarse container bound that pre-exists the system. Nothing gates sub-agent spawn.

WHERE I WAS UNCERTAIN. (1) Tier. A reasonable coder could score T2, pointing at the memcg_bpf_ops/sched_ext hooks and the container cgroup, both of which are real kernel enforcement points. I scored T3 under the weakest-link rule because the paper's contribution is the PER-TOOL-CALL domain, and entry into that domain is decided in userspace by a shim on one command interface. If the adjudicator wants to split the finding, record it as: workload-level bound T2 (pre-existing, not the contribution), per-tool-call bound T3 (the contribution). (2) Whether a co-tenant benign workload counts as an adversary at all. It is contention, not attack; A1 is the closest fit but the evaluation tests noisy-neighbor QoS, not an attacker. (3) Evidence grade. L2 is for the RESOURCE mechanism only - real prototype, real patched kernel (Linux 6.19.0-rc5 + memcg struct_ops RFC), real measurements, plus kernel selftests. No bypass was attempted and no security property was tested, so for any security-relevant reading the grade collapses to L0/L1. The authors are candid: 'Our current evaluation is limited to trace replay with a proof-of-concept prototype; the characterization covers one agent framework and one benchmark.' Evaluation ran three concurrent traces on a 4-core/16 GB machine at 50x accelerated replay - a very small scale.

COVERT-CHANNEL RULE APPLIED. Even on its own resource terms the contract has an acknowledged hole that keeps E2 off 'covered': the fine-grained domain exists only for `bash -c`, and the paper names the excluded channels itself (sub-agent, Read, Edit). Honest documentation of the gap does not close it.

MATERIAL FOR THE SoK's THREE-TIER ARGUMENT. This paper is the cleanest available illustration that 'kernel-enforced' is a property of a specific interposition point, not of a system. The enforcement primitive is unambiguously T2 and the descendant inheritance is unambiguously real - and the whole thing is still gated by a userspace shim deciding which processes get placed under it. The kernel will faithfully enforce a limit on a cgroup that a process was never put into. That is the same structural failure as the prompt's signed-capability worked example, arriving from the opposite direction: there the crypto was strong and the hook was bypassable; here the kernel is strong and the placement is bypassable.

SECONDARY PLACEMENTS, EVIDENCE. A3 (agent policy/weights) and A2 (injected context) are addressed-but-untested via the advisory hint channel: 'the agent may declare its expected resource need via an environment variable (e.g., AGENT_RESOURCE_HINT="memory:high" for a test suite, "memory:low" for a file read); the wrapper maps these to per-tool-call memory.high limits.' A mis-declaring agent - whether from a poisoned tool description (A2) or its own policy (A3) - obtains a higher ceiling by asking for one; the paper's only answer is the after-the-fact feedback loop. Untested. A4 (inside harness) and A5 (below harness) are entirely unaddressed: the bash wrapper, the user-space daemon managing cgroup lifecycle, and the shared BPF maps are all assumed trustworthy and unexamined.

SCOPE NOT CLAIMED BY THE AUTHORS. No io/blkio controller, no network controller, no LSM, no seccomp, no filesystem policy, no credential handling. Confirmed by the authors' own limitation: 'the current prototype mainly focuses on CPU and memory resource control.' E1/E3/E4/E5/E6 are not-covered as a direct consequence. E5 deserves a specific note: dependency installation appears in the paper ONLY as a memory consumer (section 3.3 lists it alongside test execution among the subprocess operations that drive memory bursts), never as a supply-chain effector - install hooks and their network activity are entirely unmediated. That sentence is deliberately NOT used as the E5 span because the range it contains rendered as a lossy character in text extraction and I could not confirm the dash codepoint; the authors' own scope limitation is quoted instead, which supports not-covered directly. E4 and E6 carry empty spans because the paper contains no sentence on VCS operations or credentials at all; per the corpus rule a cell with no span is not recorded as an evidenced claim, and both are scored not-covered by the stated default that a system which does not address an effector scores not-covered, never not-applicable.
